# Future Directions — The Cyclotomic Geometry of Knotted-Light OAM Spectra

This cycle established that, for every odd prime `p`, the `T(2, p)` torus-knot
Alexander polynomial *is* the `2p`-th cyclotomic polynomial, that its complex roots
are **exactly** the primitive `2p`-th roots of unity (no spurious roots), that its
degree — the number of orbital-angular-momentum channels — is `p − 1 = φ(2p)`, that it
is irreducible over the rationals, and that its determinant is `p` with the knot being
`3`-colorable iff it is the trefoil. The following conjectures push past the prime case.

## Conjecture 1 — The composite factorization law

For every odd `n`, the `T(2, n)` Alexander polynomial factors as
`A_n = ∏_{d | 2n, d ∤ n} Φ_d`, so its root set is the union of primitive `d`-th roots
of unity over exactly the divisors `d` of `2n` that are not divisors of `n`.

*The key insight is* that `(X + 1)·A_n = X^n + 1 = ∏_{d | 2n, d ∤ n} Φ_d`, and dividing
by the single factor `Φ_2 = X + 1` removes precisely the divisor `d = 2`, leaving a
squarefree product of cyclotomics. The prime case collapses this product to one term.

*Why now?* The exact prime-case root theorem and the fundamental identity
`(X+1)·A_n = X^n + 1` are already in hand; the composite case needs only the
divisor-set bookkeeping `{d : d | 2n} ∖ {d : d | n}`, which is a finite, checkable
combinatorial step rather than new algebra.

## Conjecture 2 — The crystalline/metallic frontier

A knot has all Alexander roots on the unit circle if and only if its Alexander
polynomial is a product of cyclotomic polynomials; among alternating knots the
smallest violator is the figure-eight, whose roots are `φ^{±2}`.

*The key insight is* that "all roots on the unit circle" for a monic reciprocal integer
polynomial is equivalent, by Kronecker's theorem, to being a product of cyclotomics
(and monomials); the figure-eight fails because `X² − 3X + 1` has discriminant `5 > 0`
placing its roots off the circle.

*Why now?* The quadratic dichotomy `b² < 4 ⇔ roots on circle` for `X² − bX + 1` is
already isolated, and the torus-knot family supplies an infinite crystalline reference
class against which off-circle behaviour can be measured.

## Conjecture 3 — Determinant equals the torsion order

For `T(2, n)` the knot determinant `|Δ(−1)| = n` equals the order of the first homology
of the double cover of `S³` branched over the knot, and `q | det` characterizes
`q`-colorability for every prime `q`.

*The key insight is* that `A_n(−1) = Σ (−(−1))^i = Σ 1 = n`, turning the determinant
into a plain channel count, and that `q`-colorability is governed by the reduction of
the Alexander module mod `q`, i.e. by `q | Δ(−1)`.

*Why now?* The identity `A_n(−1) = n` is proved, and the `3`-colorability equivalence
`3 | det ⇔ p = 3` is a proved special case; generalizing to arbitrary prime `q` needs
only the divisibility criterion `q | n`.

## Conjecture 4 — Reciprocity from a single symmetry

Every torus-knot Alexander polynomial satisfies the palindromic reciprocity
`X^{deg} · A_n(1/X) = A_n(X)`, and this is the polynomial shadow of the Seifert-form
duality `Δ(t) = det(V − tVᵀ)` with `V − Vᵀ` unimodular.

*The key insight is* that the coefficient symmetry `[X^i] = [X^{n−1−i}]` (a proved fact)
is exactly the statement that the coefficient vector is fixed by reversal, which is the
functional equation after clearing denominators.

*Why now?* The coefficient-level palindromicity is already proved for the whole family;
lifting it to the functional equation `X^{deg} A(1/X) = A(X)` is a single reindexing,
and connecting it to an abstract Seifert matrix `V` would make reciprocity uniform
across all knots rather than case-by-case.
title: That, for every odd prime `p`, the `T(2, p)` torus-knot

# Future Directions

## What was proved (this cycle)

Three self-contained Lean 4 files formalise a coherent slice of the number theory hiding inside
the quadratic recurrence `z_{n+1} = z_n^2 + c` and the Mandelbrot set.

### `MandelbrotQuadraticEscape.lean` — quantitative escape dynamics
- `qmap_norm_lower`: reverse-triangle bound `‖z‖² - ‖c‖ ≤ ‖z²+c‖`.
- `critOrbit_growth`: geometric lower bound `‖c‖·(‖c‖-1)^n ≤ ‖f_c^{(n+1)}(0)‖` when `‖c‖ > 2`.
- `critOrbit_tendsto_atTop`: the critical orbit diverges to `∞` for `‖c‖ > 2`.
- `mandelbrot_subset_closedBall`: **`M ⊆ {‖c‖ ≤ 2}`** (the classical escape-radius bound).
- Concrete membership: `0, -1 ∈ M`, `3 ∉ M`.

### `MandelbrotDoublingNumberTheory.lean` — external angles & the doubling map
- `dbl_iterate`: the `n`-th doubling is multiplication by `2^n` on `ℤ/qℤ`.
- `dbl_bijective_of_odd` / `dbl_not_injective_of_even`: periodicity of the angle `p/q` under
  doubling **iff `q` is odd**.
- `dbl_period_one`: period of `1/q` `= orderOf(2 : ZMod q)`.
- `dvd_two_pow_order_sub_one`: Mersenne-type divisibility `q ∣ 2^{period} - 1`.
- `order_two_dvd_sub_one`: for odd prime `q`, the bulb period **divides `q-1`** (Fermat).
- Contrarian disproofs: `2` is not always a primitive root (`q=7`), the period is not always
  prime (`q=5`).

### `MandelbrotFareyFibonacci.lean` — Farey/Fibonacci bulb ordering
- `fib_mediant`: consecutive Fibonacci ratios are related by the Farey mediant operation.
- `fib_cassini` + `fib_farey_neighbor`: Cassini's identity gives the unimodular Farey-neighbour
  relation between adjacent bulbs.

3. **Primitive roots / Artin.** Relate maximal bulb period (`ord_q(2) = q-1`) to Artin's
   conjecture on `2` as a primitive root; formalise density statements where tractable.
4. **Sharper escape geometry.** Upgrade `mandelbrot_subset_closedBall` to the connectedness locus
   and the `1/4`-cardioid bound `|c + 1| ≤ 1/4`-type interior estimates.
5. **Golden-mean rotation number.** Connect the Fibonacci mediant path to the continued-fraction
   expansion of the golden mean and the accumulation of satellite bulbs.

# Future Directions — Robust Neural Coding

This cycle added the **Singleton bound** and its **robust-capacity** corollary to
the neural-coding theory, complementing the earlier sphere-packing (Hamming)
ceiling. Two independent obstructions to noise-tolerant capacity are now in hand:
a *packing* obstruction (each codeword owns a Hamming ball) and a *projection*
obstruction (large minimum distance makes a few coordinates determine every
codeword). The following conjectures push the theory forward.

## 1. Perfect neural codes sit exactly where the two bounds coincide

**Conjecture.** A noise-tolerant neural codebook meets the sphere-packing bound
with equality if and only if it is a *perfect* code, and every such code also
satisfies the Singleton bound strictly unless it is a repetition or full code.

**The key insight is** that the packing ceiling and the projection ceiling are
extremal for opposite reasons — packing is tight when balls tile the cube with no
gaps, projection is tight when the code is maximally spread — so the codes that
saturate *both* are exactly the degenerate endpoints (distance `1` and distance
`N`), and everything in between saturates at most one.

**Why now?** With both ceilings formalized over the same pattern space
`Fin N → Bool`, their simultaneous equality conditions can be compared directly
rather than through separate ad-hoc arguments, making the "perfect ⇒ one bound,
not both" dichotomy precisely stateable.

## 2. Metabolic sparsity and error tolerance trade off linearly

**Conjecture.** Among weight-`k` (sparse) neural codebooks, achievable minimum
distance is capped by `d ≤ 2k`, and the resulting capacity obeys a combined
sparse-Singleton law `|C| ≤ min(C(N,k), 2^(N+1−d))`.

**The key insight is** that two sparse patterns differ in at most `2k` neurons, so
metabolic budget `k` (spikes per concept) directly limits how far apart codewords
can be pushed, coupling energy efficiency to noise tolerance in a single
inequality.

**Why now?** The exact sparse counts `C(N,k)` and the distance-based Singleton
ceiling are both available; multiplying the two constraints turns the informal
"sparse codes are cheap but fragile" intuition into a sharp frontier.

## 3. Population averaging and minimum distance give the same precision law

**Conjecture.** The `1/√N` precision of population averaging and the error
tolerance `⌊(d−1)/2⌋` of a distance-`d` code are two faces of one estimator: the
minimum-distance decoder attains mean-squared error `Θ(1/d)`, matching the
variance-of-the-mean `v/N` when `d ∝ N`.

**The key insight is** that both mechanisms fight noise by redundancy — averaging
spreads a stimulus across many neurons, distance spreads a concept across many
flippable coordinates — and their error rates should coincide once redundancy is
measured in the same units.

**Why now?** The population-variance law `v/N` and the distance-based correction
radius are now formal theorems over comparable models, so a unifying estimator
that specializes to both is within reach rather than merely analogical.

## 4. The projection argument lifts to graded (non-binary) neural alphabets

**Conjecture.** Replacing binary neurons by `q`-level firing rates yields a
`q`-ary Singleton bound `|C| ≤ q^(N+1−d)`, and the neural-manifold rank bound
becomes its continuous limit as `q → ∞`.

**The key insight is** that the puncturing/projection proof never used the
two-element structure of `Bool` — only that agreement off a `(d−1)`-set forces
distance `< d` — so it transfers verbatim to any finite alphabet and, in the
limit, to the linear-rank ceiling of the manifold hypothesis.

**Why now?** The proof here is already alphabet-agnostic in spirit; isolating the
one place binariness is used shows it is inessential, opening a direct bridge from
discrete coding bounds to the continuous neural-manifold dimension bound.

# Future Directions

`Bridges/RamanujanBaireBridge.lean` builds a cross-domain bridge for the Ramanujan
oracle program: it recasts the **counting/diagonalization** obstruction to computable
oracles as a **Baire-category (topological genericity)** statement on the Cantor space
`ℕ → Bool`.

## What is proved

- `perfect_unique`: an oracle is perfect for at most one ground truth.
- `singleton_notMem_nhds`: the Cantor space `ℕ → Bool` has no isolated points.
- `isNowhereDense_singleton`, `isNowhereDense_of_subsingleton`: singletons and
  subsingletons are nowhere dense there.
- `covered_isMeagre`: for any **countable** family of oracles, the set of ground truths
  that some oracle decides perfectly is **meagre**.
- `missed_dense` / `missed_residual`: the set of ground truths defeating the entire
  family is **dense / comeager** — a strict topological sharpening of "uncountably
  many truths escape".
- `missed_nonempty`: existence of a defeating truth, now obtained via the Baire
  category theorem rather than a cardinality count.
- `countable_computable_oracles`: there are only countably many `Computable` oracles.
- `defeating_computable_comeager`, `missed_computable_dense`,
  `exists_truth_no_computable_perfect`: a **topologically generic** ground truth
  defeats *every computable oracle at once*.

The connector: Cantor's diagonal against a countable list of oracles is not an ad hoc
trick — the winning "diagonal" truths form a residual (Baire-generic) set.

## Directions to deepen

1. **Measure-theoretic twin.** Replace category by measure: under the uniform
   Bernoulli(1/2) product measure on `ℕ → Bool`, each perfect set is a single point
   (null, since the measure is atomless), so the covered set is null and the defeating
   set has full measure. This would give the measure/category dual of the same bridge.

2. **Quantitative genericity.** Strengthen "comeager" to an explicit dense `Gδ`
   description of the defeating set, and estimate the "size" of the finite cylinders
   needed to diagonalize the first `k` oracles.

3. **Relativized oracles.** Extend the countability bridge from `Computable` functions
   to `ComputablePred` and to oracle Turing machines with relativized queries, keeping
   the topological conclusion (`missed_dense`) intact.

4. **Effective genericity.** Connect to the recursion-theoretic notion of *1-generic*
   reals: the defeating truths against a uniformly computable family should include a
   `1`-generic, tying the Baire-category argument to effective descriptive set theory.

5. **Beyond Bool.** Generalize the base space from `ℕ → Bool` to `ℕ → Fin (k+2)` or
   `ℕ → α` for a finite discrete `α` with `2 ≤ card α`, where the no-isolated-points
   argument and hence the whole bridge still applies.

# Future Directions

This cycle unified two threshold phenomena — mean-field magnetic ordering
(`m = tanh(β m)`) and branching-process survival (`q = 1 - exp(-μ q)`) — under a
single abstract criterion: a concave increasing map through the origin acquires a
positive fixed point exactly when its origin-slope crosses `1`. The abstract
existence lemma generates both ordered phases, and the *symmetry* of the update
map was shown to control the critical exponent (`1/2` for the odd magnetic map,
`1` for the asymmetric offspring map). The following conjectures extend this
programme.

## 1. A symmetry–exponent dictionary for order parameters

**Conjecture.** For an order parameter obeying `x = F(x)` with `F` smooth,
increasing, concave on `[0, ∞)`, `F(0) = 0`, and origin-slope `1 + ε`, the onset
exponent is `1/2` precisely when `F` is odd (so the leading correction is cubic)
and `1` when `F` has a nonzero quadratic term; more generally, if the first
nonvanishing correction beyond the linear term is of order `k`, the exponent is
`1/(k-1)`.

The key insight is that the onset exponent is not a property of the physical
model but of the lowest surviving Taylor coefficient of the fixed-point map, so
a single Taylor-coefficient bookkeeping predicts every mean-field exponent at
once.

Why now? Both endpoints of the dictionary (`k = 3` giving `1/2`, `k = 2` giving
`1`) are now established in the same framework with matching two-sided algebraic
bounds, so the intermediate cases are within reach of the identical
bracketing technique.

## 2. Sharp two-sided asymptotics for branching survival

**Conjecture.** The Poisson branching survival probability satisfies
`q*(μ) = 2(μ - 1) - (8/3)(μ - 1)² + o((μ - 1)²)` as `μ → 1⁺`, and `q*` is a
real-analytic, strictly increasing function of `μ` on `(1, ∞)` with
`q*(μ) → 1` as `μ → ∞`.

The key insight is that the quadratic and cubic exponential bounds already used
for the linear lower bound can be iterated to pin the second-order coefficient,
turning a one-sided estimate into a full local expansion.

Why now? The linear coefficient `2` is confirmed numerically to four digits and
the required exponential inequalities (`x - x²/2 < 1 - e^{-x}` and its cubic
refinement) are elementary and already in hand.

## 3. Uniqueness of the field-perturbed branch

**Conjecture.** For the externally-driven equations `m = tanh(β m + h)` and the
immigration-perturbed survival equation `q = 1 - exp(-(μ q + h))` with `h > 0`,
the positive solution is unique for every coupling, so the sharp threshold is
replaced by a single analytic branch and a line of first-order transitions that
terminates at the critical point `(coupling, h) = (1, 0)`.

The key insight is that a strictly positive field turns the fixed-point map into
a strict contraction on the relevant interval, so uniqueness follows from the
same mean-value argument that already yields uniqueness of the zero-field
positive branch.

Why now? Existence under a positive field is already settled for the magnetic
model, and the branching model shares the identical concavity structure, so only
the contraction estimate remains.

## 4. Percolation on regular trees

**Conjecture.** Bond percolation with retention probability `p` on the rooted
`d`-ary tree has a giant (infinite) cluster from the root with positive
probability if and only if `p d > 1`, and the survival probability obeys the same
abstract fixed-point dichotomy with coupling `μ = p d`, hence the same universal
critical value and the same linear onset exponent.

The key insight is that the root-cluster survival probability is exactly the
survival probability of a binomial branching process, so the tree percolation
threshold is a direct instance of the branching dichotomy rather than a separate
theorem.

Why now? The Poisson case is fully established here, and the binomial offspring
map `1 - (1 - p q)^d` satisfies the identical hypotheses (concave, increasing,
origin-slope `pd`), so it plugs directly into the abstract existence lemma.

## 5. Variational characterization via free energy

**Conjecture.** The stable order parameter of each model is the global minimizer
of an associated free-energy functional — `m²/2 - β⁻¹ log cosh(β m)` for the
magnet and a Kullback–Leibler-type rate function for the branching survival —
and the minimal free energy is analytic in the coupling away from the critical
value and non-analytic exactly at it.

The key insight is that both self-consistency equations are the stationarity
conditions of a convex-minus-linear functional, so the fixed-point dichotomy is
the shadow of a genuine change in the geometry of the minimizer set.

Why now? The fixed-point side is completely characterized (existence,
uniqueness, quantitative onset), which supplies precisely the critical-point data
needed to control the minimizer and locate the single point of non-analyticity.
title: This cycle unified two threshold phenomena — mean-field magnetic ordering

# Future Directions — Tightness of the Isolation Lemma bound

The exact count established for the singleton hypergraph shows that the global
lower bound `n · ∑_{j=0}^{d-1} j^{n-1}` on the number of isolating weight
assignments is attained on the nose by a concrete inclusion-free hypergraph.
This pins down the extremal value and motivates the following bold, testable
conjectures.

## Conjecture 1 — Per-hypergraph tightness under offsets

For every inclusion-free hypergraph `H` on `n` vertices there is an edge offset
function `f` so that the number of isolating assignments in `[d]^n` equals
exactly `n · ∑_{j=0}^{d-1} j^{n-1}`.

The key insight is that a generic offset flattens the hypergraph's internal
comparisons so that isolation is governed solely by a single controlling vertex
per assignment, reproducing the singleton-hypergraph count. Why now? The exact
singleton identity supplies the precise target value and the vertex-argmin
decomposition needed to transport the count to arbitrary Sperner families.

## Conjecture 2 — Rigidity of the extremizers

The offsets `f` achieving the exact minimum count form a positive-measure,
polyhedrally described region of offset space, and every extremizer induces the
same argmin-partition statistics as the singleton hypergraph.

The key insight is that attaining the bound forces a unique-minimum structure
almost everywhere, which is a closed linear condition on the offsets. Why now?
Having the exact extremal value converts "is the bound tight?" into a concrete
polytope-nonemptiness question amenable to explicit description.

## Conjecture 3 — A strict gap away from Sperner families

If `H` fails to be inclusion-free, then for every offset `f` the number of
isolating assignments is strictly less than `n · ∑_{j=0}^{d-1} j^{n-1}` for all
sufficiently large `d`.

The key insight is that a containment `S ⊊ T` permanently couples two edges'
weights, destroying the independence that the extremal count relies on. Why now?
The proved identity isolates exactly which structural feature (incomparability)
the extremal count uses, making the failure mode precise and falsifiable.

## Conjecture 4 — Refined power-sum decomposition

For every `n`, the extremal count `n · ∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}`, viewed as a polynomial
in `d`, has all of its nonnegative-integer roots at `d = 0, 1`, and its leading
behaviour `n · d^n / n = d^n / 1` reflects a clean bijective decomposition of
isolating assignments by (argmin vertex, minimum value).

The key insight is that the term `∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}` is the exact fiber size over a
fixed argmin, so the polynomial's arithmetic mirrors the combinatorial fibering.
Why now? The verified fiberwise count makes the polynomial identity a direct
corollary rather than a numerical coincidence.

# Future Directions — Neural Coding: from Averages to Concentration

The present cycle upgraded the neural-coding chain from *first-moment* facts
(capacity `2^N`, average energy `N/2`, sparse counts `C(N,k)`, population
precision `1/√N`) to a *full concentration* statement: the metabolic weight of a
dense code has variance exactly `N/4`, and at least three quarters of all codes
lie within `√N` of the mean `N/2`. The weight is a Binomial(N, 1/2) in disguise,
so the population energy obeys a law of large numbers. The following conjectures
push this "moments → concentration → geometry" programme further.

## 1. Sub-Gaussian (exponential) energy concentration

**Conjecture.** The fraction of codes whose weight deviates from `N/2` by at
least `t` decays like `exp(−2t²/N)`, not merely `N/(4t²)`; consequently, for any
fixed `ε > 0`, all but an exponentially small fraction of codes have weight in
`[(1/2−ε)N, (1/2+ε)N]`.

The key insight is that the coordinates of a binary code are independent bounded
contributions, so the weight is not just a variance-`N/4` variable but a genuine
sum of independent `±` increments, and the exponential moment — not the second
moment — is the sharp instrument. Chebyshev sees only the second moment; the
correct object is the log-moment-generating function of a single neuron.

Why now? The exact second moment established this cycle is the first term of the
cumulant expansion; having pinned it down, the natural next step is to control
the whole cumulant sequence and convert the polynomial tail into an exponential
one, which immediately sharpens every downstream capacity estimate.

## 2. Energy–distance trade-off for noise-tolerant codebooks

**Conjecture.** Any codebook with minimum Hamming distance `d` whose codewords
all have weight near `N/2` (within `o(√N)`) satisfies a strictly stronger size
bound than the generic Singleton ceiling `2^(N+1−d)`; concentrating the energy
budget forces the codewords into a thin equatorial shell whose limited volume
caps the codebook.

The key insight is that the concentration result says the overwhelming majority
of patterns already live near the equator, so a large-distance codebook cannot
also be energy-balanced without competing for the *same* scarce shell that
carries most of the mass — packing and balancing pull against each other.

Why now? With both the Singleton projection ceiling and the exact weight
concentration in hand, the two constraints can finally be imposed
simultaneously, turning a qualitative tension into a quantitative shell-volume
bound.

## 3. Concentration of the population-coding error

**Conjecture.** When `N` neurons independently estimate a stimulus, not only
does the mean squared error scale like `1/N`, but the *realised* error
concentrates around its mean: the probability that the population estimate is off
by more than `c/√N` decays polynomially in `N` for every constant `c`, so the
`1/√N` precision law holds pattern-by-pattern, not only on average.

The key insight is that the same variance-of-the-mean algebra that produced the
`1/√N` law also controls the fourth moment of the averaged estimate, and a
second-moment bound on the *squared* error upgrades an average guarantee into a
high-probability one.

Why now? The population-precision law and the weight-variance computation share
one algebraic engine — the independence of the `N` contributions — so the
concentration machinery just proved for weights transfers directly to the
estimator error.

## 4. Dimension of the concentrated neural manifold

**Conjecture.** If population activity is driven by `d` behavioural degrees of
freedom through a generic bounded map, then not only is the neural manifold's
dimension at most `d`, but the reachable activity concentrates on an
`d`-dimensional shell of radius `Θ(√N)`; the effective, energy-weighted
dimension is exactly `d` even though the ambient space has dimension `N`.

The key insight is that concentration of the raw activity (weights near `N/2`)
and the linear-algebraic dimension cap combine: the manifold is not merely
low-dimensional but sits at a fixed metabolic radius, so its "thickness" in the
energy direction vanishes relative to `√N`.

Why now? The dimension bound and the energy concentration were proved
separately; overlaying them is the natural synthesis, and it predicts a testable
geometric signature — a fixed-radius, low-dimensional activity shell — for
recorded population data.

# Future Directions: Homological Quantum Codes — Cycle 1 results

Thread `th_c942ee26`, root direction `fd_0859`. The previous cycle established
the exact dictionary **"logical qubits = middle homology"** for the length-two
chain-complex model of CSS codes (`CSSComplex.numLogical_add`,
`CSSComplex.euler`) and used it to refute the folklore "one qubit" law for the
hypercube *graph* (`Hypercube.betti1_closed`, `betti1_eq_one_iff`).

This cycle settles **all four** stated conjectures with complete Lean 4
proofs. Conjectures 2–4 are field-agnostic and use the additive form of
rank–nullity (no truncated ℕ-subtraction); see `LogicalDimension.lean`.
Conjecture 1 (distance = girth = 4) is settled in `HypercubeGirth.lean`.

## Results proved this cycle

### Conjecture 3 — Realizability of every logical/physical pair ✔ PROVED
- `ChainCplx.realizable_pair` : for every field `K` and all `p k : ℕ`, there is a
  length-two complex with `dim B = p + k` and logical dimension **exactly** `k`.
- `ChainCplx.realizable_le` : for every field `K` and every `k ≤ n`, a complex
  with physical dimension exactly `n` and logical dimension exactly `k` exists —
  every `(n, k)` pair is realized.
- `ChainCplx.realizable_ranks` (refined form matching the conjecture's insight):
  for all `r s m : ℕ` there is a complex with `dim B = r + s + m`,
  `rank d₁ = r`, `rank d₂ = s`, and logical dimension exactly `m`. This turns the
  exact accounting `k = dim B − rank d₁ − rank d₂` into a rank-prescription
  construction (`B = Kʳ × Kˢ × Kᵐ`, `d₁ = fst`, `d₂ = inclusion of the middle
  factor`).

### Conjecture 4 — Cohomological / CSS self-duality ✔ PROVED
- `ChainCplx.dual` : the transposed complex `C* --d₁ᵀ--> B* --d₂ᵀ--> A*`.
- `ChainCplx.numLogical_dual` : `X.dual.numLogical = X.numLogical`. The
  `X`-logical space `ker d₁ / im d₂` and the `Z`-logical space
  `ker d₂ᵀ / im d₁ᵀ` always have equal dimension. The proof is exactly the
  rank symmetry `rank fᵀ = rank f` (`LinearMap.finrank_range_dualMap_eq_finrank_range`)
  fed through the dimension formula, plus `dim B* = dim B` for finite spaces.

### Conjecture 2 — Euler characteristic as a code rate ✔ PROVED (formula + endpoints)
- `ChainCplx.graph_count` : for a connected graph complex (`d₂ = 0`, `β₀ = 1`)
  with `V = dim C`, `E = dim B`, one has `k + V = E + 1`.
- `ChainCplx.rate_eq` : the code rate `k / E` equals `1 − (V−1)/E` (for `E > 0`).
- `ChainCplx.rate_tree` : a tree (`E = V − 1`) has `k = 0`, rate `0`.
- `ChainCplx.rate_bouquet` : a one-vertex bouquet (`V = 1`) has `k = E`, rate `1`.
  These pin the extremes of the rate; the endpoints are exactly the trees
  (minimum) and bouquets (maximum) named in the conjecture.

### Conjecture 1 — distance = girth = 4 ✔ PROVED
Formalized in `HypercubeGirth.lean`. The hypercube graph `Qₙ` is modelled as the
Mathlib `SimpleGraph` on vertex set `Fin n → ZMod 2` with adjacency "differ in
exactly one coordinate" (`HomQECC.hypercube`). For a one-dimensional (graph)
complex the homological minimum distance is the length of a shortest nontrivial
cycle, i.e. the graph **girth**, so Conjecture 1 reduces to `girth Qₙ = 4`.

- `HomQECC.parity` / `HomQECC.parity_adj` : the coordinate-sum parity is a proper
  2-colouring — adjacent vertices differ in parity.
- `HomQECC.hypercube_walk_length_parity` : along any walk the endpoint parity is
  the start parity plus the walk length (`Qₙ` is bipartite).
- `HomQECC.hypercube_closed_walk_even` / `HomQECC.hypercube_triangle_free` : every
  closed walk has even length, so there is no `3`-cycle (girth `≥ 4`).
- `HomQECC.hypercube_has_four_cycle` : for `n ≥ 2` the explicit square
  `0 → e₀ → e₀+e₁ → e₁ → 0` is a `4`-cycle (girth `≤ 4`).
- `HomQECC.hypercube_girth` : `girth Qₙ = 4` for all `n ≥ 2`, independent of `n`.
- `HomQECC.singleton_gap` : `4 < 2^{n/2}` (as a real power) for `n ≥ 5`, so the
  constant girth distance `4` is strictly below the quantum Singleton value
  `2^{n/2}`; the hypercube homological code does **not** achieve the quantum
  Singleton bound for `n ≥ 5`.

All theorems in `HypercubeGirth.lean` depend only on `propext`,
`Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`.

## Notes
- `HypercubeGirth.lean` is self-contained (`import Mathlib` only) and models `Qₙ`
  directly on `Fin n → ZMod 2` via Mathlib's `SimpleGraph`/`girth`.
- `LogicalDimension.lean` is self-contained (`import Mathlib` only) and reproves
  the core dimension identities in its own namespace `HomQECC` so it compiles
  independently of the previous cycle's `CSSHomology.lean` / `HypercubeCode.lean`.
- All headline theorems depend only on `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`.

# Future Directions — Divisor-Stratified OAM Spectra of Torus Knots

This cycle established the general divisor factorization of the `T(2,n)` Alexander
polynomial: for every odd `n`,

  A_n(X) = ∏_{d ∣ n, d > 1} Φ_{2d}(X),

so the orbital-angular-momentum (OAM) spectrum of a `T(2,n)` knotted-light beam is a
disjoint union of primitive-root layers, one layer of primitive `2d`-th roots of unity
for each nontrivial divisor `d ∣ n`. The total channel count is `n − 1` and the number
of layers is `τ(n) − 1`; a single layer occurs exactly when `n` is prime. The following
conjectures are natural, bold, and testable continuations.

## 1. Galois-orbit stratification is a spectral fingerprint

**Conjecture.** Two `T(2,m)` and `T(2,n)` beams have OAM spectra related by a field
automorphism if and only if `m` and `n` have the same multiset of nontrivial divisors,
i.e. `m = n`. Consequently the unordered layer list `{2d : d ∣ n, d > 1}` is a complete
invariant of the beam within the `T(2,·)` family.

The key insight is that each layer is an *irreducible* Galois orbit (a cyclotomic
factor), so the spectrum decomposes canonically into indivisible pieces indexed by the
divisor lattice, and the lattice of `n` is recoverable from the layer degrees `φ(2d)`.

Why now? The exact, no-spurious-roots description of each layer as the primitive
`2d`-th roots of unity makes the orbit decomposition rigorous, turning a heuristic
"spectral fingerprint" into a precise reconstruction problem.

## 2. The metallic exception is intrinsically non-cyclotomic

**Conjecture.** Among all knots whose Alexander polynomial is monic with unit constant
term and degree ≤ 2, the figure-eight `4₁` is the unique one whose roots avoid the unit
circle; equivalently, `X² − 3X + 1` is the only such polynomial whose roots are a
metallic pair `(φ², φ^{-2})` rather than a cyclotomic pair.

The key insight is that the quadratic palindrome `X² − bX + 1` is crystalline (roots on
the unit circle) exactly when `|b| ≤ 1` and metallic (real reciprocal roots) exactly
when `|b| ≥ 2`, with no intermediate regime; `b = 3` for `4₁` sits strictly in the
metallic zone while every `T(2,p)` sits at `b = 1`.

Why now? The divisor factorization pins the torus family entirely on the unit circle,
sharpening the contrast with `4₁` into a clean dichotomy that can be scanned across
larger knot tables.

## 3. Prime-power beams are self-similar under harmonic zoom

**Conjecture.** For an odd prime `p`, the `T(2, p^{k+1})` OAM spectrum is obtained from
the `T(2, p^k)` spectrum by adjoining a single new outer layer of primitive
`2p^{k+1}`-th roots of unity, and the map `ζ ↦ ζ^p` carries layer `j+1` onto layer `j`.
Hence the spectrum is exactly self-similar under a `p`-fold angular rescaling.

The key insight is that the divisors of `p^k` form a chain `1 ∣ p ∣ p² ∣ ⋯ ∣ p^k`, so
the factorization is a nested tower `Φ_{2p}, Φ_{2p²}, …` rather than an unstructured
product, and the Frobenius-type map `ζ ↦ ζ^p` realises the tower's shift.

Why now? With the prime-power stratification made explicit, the shift map becomes a
concrete construction on the finite layer set instead of an asymptotic statement.

## 4. Channel capacity is additive over coprime knot connect-sums

**Conjecture.** If `m` and `n` are coprime odd integers, the OAM layer set of the beam
associated to `mn` is the union of the layer sets attached to the divisor lattices of
`m` and `n`, glued along their shared "mixed" divisors, and the total channel count
satisfies `deg A_{mn} = mn − 1`, strictly larger than `(m − 1) + (n − 1)`.

The key insight is that the divisor lattice of a product of coprimes is the product of
the lattices, so layers multiply combinatorially; the excess `mn − 1 − (m−1) − (n−1) =
(m−1)(n−1)` measures the genuinely new "cross" layers `Φ_{2d}` for `d` a nontrivial
mixed divisor.

Why now? The factorization is indexed by divisors, so coprime multiplicativity of the
divisor function immediately predicts the new layers, giving a falsifiable count that
can be checked against any tabulated connect-sum invariant.

## 5. Determinant growth tracks the smallest prime factor

**Conjecture.** The knot determinant `|A_n(−1)| = n` of `T(2,n)` is divisible by `3` if
and only if the trefoil layer `Φ₆` is present, i.e. if and only if `3 ∣ n`; more
generally, for each odd prime `q`, the layer `Φ_{2q}` is present exactly when `q ∣ n`,
so the layer set reads off the prime factorization of the determinant.

The key insight is that `A_n(−1) = n` is a plain alternating count, while the layer set
is indexed by divisors of `n`, so primality tests on the determinant translate directly
into presence/absence of specific cyclotomic layers.

Why now? With both the determinant formula and the divisor-indexed layer set proven for
the whole family, the correspondence between arithmetic of the determinant and the
geometry of the spectrum is exact and immediately checkable.

# Future Directions — Clique Densities

This cycle established the unconditional *upper* comparison of clique counts,
`C(t,s)·k_t(G) ≤ C(n-s,t-s)·k_s(G)`, its tightness on the complete graph, and the
resulting antitonicity of the normalized clique density `k_r(G)/C(n,r)`. These
findings sharpen the picture of how clique counts of different orders constrain one
another and motivate the following bold, testable conjectures.

## 1. The sharp clique-to-clique lower bound

For all integers `2 ≤ s < t` and every `n`-vertex graph `G`,
`k_t(G)/n^t ≥ F_t(F_s^{-1}(k_s(G)/n^s))`,
where `F_r` is the Lovász–Simonovits function tracing the minimum `r`-clique density
along the sequence of balanced complete multipartite graphs, and `F_s^{-1}` is its
generalized inverse. The case `s = 2` is Reiher's clique density theorem.

**The key insight is** that while the *upper* comparison is governed by the complete
graph (a single clique), the matching *lower* bound is governed by complete
multipartite graphs, so the extremal transition from `s`-cliques to `t`-cliques is
captured exactly by composing the two piecewise-linear/convex density profiles.

**Why now?** The unconditional upper bound and its tightness certificate isolate the
complete graph as the only equality case, cleanly separating the two extremal
regimes; this separation is precisely the structural hypothesis needed to attack the
lower bound by an averaging-and-symmetrization argument over multipartite parts.

## 2. Stability of the antitone density profile

If `k_t(G)/C(n,t)` is within `ε` of `k_s(G)/C(n,s)` for some `s < t`, then `G` is
`o(1)`-close (in edit distance per vertex pair) to a disjoint union of cliques.

**The key insight is** that equality in the normalized-density antitonicity forces
every `s`-clique to extend to the full number `C(n-s,t-s)` of `t`-cliques, which can
only happen if the neighborhoods align into complete blocks.

**Why now?** The exact equality analysis of the count bound already pins down the
complete graph; a robust, quantitative version is the natural next step and would
give a clique-decomposition analogue of the triangle-removal phenomenon.

## 3. Weighted and fractional clique densities

The antitonicity `k_t/C(n,t) ≤ k_s/C(n,s)` extends to weighted graphons: for a
symmetric measurable `W : [0,1]^2 → [0,1]`, the homomorphism densities `t(K_r, W)`
satisfy a corresponding monotone relation after normalization by the clique moments.

**The key insight is** that the finite double-counting incidence identity has a
continuous avatar as a Fubini exchange between the `s`-fold and `t`-fold clique
integrals of `W`, so the discrete inequality survives the limit.

**Why now?** Graphon limits make the `n → ∞` behavior of the density profile a
first-class object, and the exact finite identity proved here transfers verbatim,
providing an immediately checkable continuous conjecture.

## 4. Beyond cliques: monotone density profiles for general subgraphs

For a fixed graph `H` and its `r`-vertex "blow-up truncations" `H_r`, the normalized
subgraph-count profile `hom(H_r, G)/hom(H_r, K_n)` is antitone in `r` whenever the
`H_r` form a subset-closed tower.

**The key insight is** that the only property of cliques used in the count bound is
that a sub-object of a clique is again a clique; any subset-closed family of dense
patterns inherits the same incidence double count.

**Why now?** Subset-closedness is exactly the combinatorial hypothesis that the
present proof isolates, so generalizing away from cliques is a matter of identifying
the right closed towers rather than inventing new machinery.
title: Unconditional *upper* comparison of clique counts,

# Future Directions

## Summary of what was proved / disproved

File: `Catalog/Applications/RBDomainContrarian.lean` (self-contained, no `sorry`,
axioms: `propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound` only).

We work with the combinatorial shadow of the Jung–Tix characterization: a finite
poset `P` is **RB-shaped** when it has a least element and its undirected Hasse
graph is a tree (`RBShape P := HasLeast P ∧ (hasseGraph P).IsTree`). The
genuinely domain-theoretic notions (probabilistic valuations, probabilistic
powerdomain, RB = retract-of-bifinite) are outside Mathlib; `RBShape` is exactly
the two-conjunct condition the characterization attributes to such posets.

**Reusable core (proved).**
- `diamond_not_isAcyclic`: any poset containing a covering diamond
  `a ⋖ b, a ⋖ c, b ⋖ d, c ⋖ d` with `b ≠ c` has a **non-acyclic** Hasse graph.
  Proof: the two length-2 paths `a–b–d` and `a–c–d` are distinct paths with equal
  endpoints, contradicting acyclicity's unique-path criterion.
- Corollaries `diamond_not_isTree`, `diamond_not_rbShape`.

**Conjecture A — refuted.** *"A finite poset with a least element is RB-shaped."*
- `least_not_sufficient_for_rbShape`: the diamond `Bool × Bool` (the `2×2`
  Boolean lattice) has least element `(false,false)` but is **not** RB-shaped,
  because its Hasse graph carries the covering diamond above (a 4-cycle). This is
  the classical **Jung–Tix diamond obstruction** in combinatorial form: a least
  element alone does not deliver the tree structure.

**Conjecture B — refuted.** *"A finite poset whose Hasse graph is acyclic (a
forest) has a least element."*
- `forest_not_sufficient_for_hasLeast`: the two-element antichain `Anti2` has an
  edgeless (hence acyclic) Hasse graph but **no** least element.

**Conjecture B — sharpened to a genuine tree (proved).** *"Even a Hasse graph
that is a genuine tree (connected and acyclic), not merely a forest, has a least
element."* Also refuted.
- `tree_not_sufficient_for_hasLeast`: the three-element **"V" poset** `V3`
  (`a, b` incomparable minimal, both covered by a top `c`) has Hasse graph the
  path `a – c – b`, which is a genuine tree (`v3_hasseGraph_isTree`:
  `SimpleGraph.IsTree`, i.e. connected *and* acyclic), yet `V3` has no least
  element (`v3_not_hasLeast`). This strengthens
  `forest_not_sufficient_for_hasLeast` from "forest" to "tree", closing the
  former open direction #1.

**Positive sanity check (proved).**
- `bool_rbShape`: the two-element chain `Bool` **is** RB-shaped, so `RBShape` is
  not vacuous and both conjuncts are simultaneously realizable.

Net contrarian message: neither conjunct of the RB-shape condition implies the
other, and neither alone implies RB-shape — the diamond and the antichain are
the minimal witnesses for the two independent failures.

## Open directions

1. **Connected tree without a least element — DONE.** The "V"/Λ poset (`a, b < c`,
   with `a, b` incomparable) has a Hasse graph that is a *genuine tree*
   (connected, 2 edges on 3 vertices) yet has no least element. This is now
   formalized as `tree_not_sufficient_for_hasLeast` / `v3_hasseGraph_isTree`.
   Rather than the Euler edge-count route (blocked because
   `SimpleGraph.edgeFinset` is non-computable), acyclicity is discharged
   structurally via `SimpleGraph.isAcyclic_iff_forall_adj_isBridge` together with
   `SimpleGraph.isBridge_iff` and `decide` on the finite adjacency, and
   connectivity via `SimpleGraph.connected_iff_exists_forall_reachable`.

2. **General chains.** Prove that *every* nonempty finite linear order is
   RB-shaped (connectivity follows from the least element; acyclicity needs the
   monotone-path uniqueness argument). Only the 2-chain is formalized here.

3. **Tree ⇔ diamond-free (finite posets).** Conjecture: for a finite poset with
   a least element, the Hasse graph is a tree **iff** the poset is
   *diamond-free* (no covering diamond `a ⋖ b, a ⋖ c, b ⋖ d, c ⋖ d`, `b ≠ c`).
   The "not diamond-free ⇒ not tree" direction is exactly `diamond_not_isTree`;
   the converse (a shortest Hasse cycle in a poset with `⊥` forces a diamond)
   is the interesting open half.

4. **A lattice with tree Hasse graph is a chain.** Conjecture: a finite lattice
   whose Hasse graph is a tree must be totally ordered. Two incomparable
   elements would produce a diamond via their meet/join, closing a cycle.

5. **Bridging to the actual powerdomain.** The above are combinatorial shadows.
   A genuine formalization of the Jung–Tix result requires developing
   probabilistic valuations, the probabilistic powerdomain, and RB-domains in
   Lean — substantial infrastructure not yet present in Mathlib.

# Future directions — Isolation-Lemma tightness for arbitrary edge offsets

This cycle deepened the singleton-hypergraph tightness result of
`IsolationLemmaTightness.lean`. New Lean file:
`IsolationLemmaTightnessArbitraryOffsets.lean`.

## What was settled this cycle

1. **The general tightness conjecture is FALSE** (`general_tightness_fails`).
   It is *not* true that every inclusion-free hypergraph attains the Faber–Harris
   bound `n·∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}` for some real offset. A single-edge hypergraph makes
   every assignment isolating, giving count `d^n` for *all* offsets `f`, strictly
   above the bound (already `4 > 2` at `n=d=2`). Offset freedom does not repair an
   over-counting hypergraph.

2. **A new symmetric extremal witness** (`card_strictMax_eq`). The co-singleton
   hypergraph (all `(n-1)`-edges) *also* attains the bound exactly with zero
   offset, via a min↔max reflection duality (`hasStrictMin_iff_rev`,
   `card_strictMax_eq_card_isolating`). Thus the bound has at least two
   symmetric extremal witnesses (singletons and their complements).

## Open questions raised

- **Characterise the extremal hypergraphs.** Computation for `n=3` shows exactly
  the singletons and the all-pairs (co-singleton) families reach the bound.
  Conjecture: for the *offset-free* problem, an antichain attains `B(n,d)` iff it
  is vertex-transitive and "sum-symmetric" (e.g. the `k`-uniform complete designs
  for suitable `k`). A formal characterisation is open.

- **Covering antichains still fail.** Even covering antichains such as
  `{{0,1},{0,2}}` overshoot the bound for every offset (verified computationally,
  excess ≥ 1). A formal proof of failure that quantifies over *all real offsets*
  (not just the degenerate single-edge case) would strengthen
  `general_tightness_fails`. The obstacle is reducing the continuum of offsets to
  the finite set of order-types; a Lean development of that reduction is the
  natural next step.

- **Which `k`-uniform complete hypergraphs are extremal?** The singletons (`k=1`)
  and co-singletons (`k=n-1`) are extremal. Are the complete `k`-uniform families
  extremal for intermediate `k`? Preliminary data suggests not in general; a clean
  criterion is open.

- **Quantitative excess.** Define `excess(H) := min_f #isolating(H,f) − B(n,d) ≥ 0`.
  Understanding `excess` as a hypergraph invariant (monotonicity, additivity under
  disjoint unions) is an appealing direction.

# Future Directions — Causal Loops in Category Theory

Mission: *"Causal Loops in Category Theory: when composition loops back"* — a tensor
product whose associativity fails **on the nose** but is repaired by a canonical
invertible `2`-cell (the associator), with coherence holding automatically.

## What this cycle adds

**`Catalog/Novelty/MonoidalStrictification.lean` — the monoidal strictification
theorem for the parenthesization category.**

This is the natural next step of Direction 1 from the previous cycle ("upgrade
`strictify` to a *monoidal* equivalence"). The file is fully self-contained
(`import Mathlib` only) and re-establishes the thin-category engine and the
parenthesization category before carrying out the monoidal upgrade. It builds a single
chain of results, each using the previous one:

1. `ThinCategory`, `monoidalOfThin` — coherence is free on a thin category.
2. `PTree`, `flatten` (valued in `FreeMonoid α`), `instMonoidalCategory` — the
   non-strict parenthesization monoidal category.
3. `flatten_tensor`, `flatten_unit` — flattening strictly respects tensor and unit
   (both by `rfl`).
4. `flattenFunctor`, `flattenCore`, `instFlattenMonoidal` — flattening is a **strong
   monoidal functor** into `Discrete (FreeMonoid α)` (Mathlib's `Discrete.monoidal`,
   concatenation as tensor).
5. `strictify` — the underlying categorical equivalence
   `PTree α ≌ Discrete (FreeMonoid α)`.
6. `strictify_functor_monoidal`, `strictify_inverse_monoidal`, `strictify_isMonoidal`
   — **the monoidal strictification theorem**: `PTree α` is *monoidally* equivalent to
   its strict skeleton. The inverse's monoidal structure and the compatibility
   (`IsMonoidal`) are obtained via Mathlib's `Equivalence.inverseMonoidal`.
7. `flatten_associator_to_id` — under strictification the associator loop becomes an
   identity-type morphism: the causal loop is contracted.

All main results are checked to depend only on the standard axioms
(`propext`, `Classical.choice`, `Quot.sound`) and contain no `sorry`.

This realizes, for this concrete family, the full statement of **Mac Lane's
strictification theorem**: a coherent (loop-tolerant) monoidal structure is monoidally
equivalent to a strict (loop-free) one.

## Remaining directions to extend

1. **Braided / symmetric layer.** `Discrete (FreeMonoid α)` is not braided in general
   (concatenation is noncommutative), but `Discrete (Multiset α)` /
   `Discrete (List α)`-with-a-braiding gives a symmetric target; study whether the
   flattening functor can be promoted to a braided monoidal functor onto a commutative
   quotient.

2. **Unitors and a coherent unit.** Analyse the unit-coherence loops (`triangle`) in the
   same thin framework and compare with the Saavedra/Kelly redundancy of the unit axioms.

3. **Bicategorical version.** Feed `PTree α` through the delooping
   (`EndMonoidal` / `MonoidalSingleObj`) to produce an explicit one-object bicategory
   whose horizontal composition is non-associative on the nose, then transport the
   monoidal strictification to a bicategorical strictification.

4. **Non-thin obstructions.** Exhibit a non-thin `MonoidalCategoryStruct` where the
   pentagon fails, quantifying how thinness is exactly the boundary between free and
   obstructed coherence.

5. **Free monoidal category.** Relate `PTree α` to Mathlib's `FreeMonoidalCategory`:
   `PTree α` is the free monoidal category on the discrete category `α` *quotiented by
   coherence*, and the monoidal `strictify` above exhibits its strict skeleton.

# Future Directions — Automatic Sequences and the Kernel Criterion

This cycle established the finite-kernel criterion for automatic sequences as a
self-contained, characteristic-free foundation: decimations compose by a single
semigroup law, the resulting kernel is closed under decimation, and the class of
automatic sequences (over a fixed base) is closed under constants, output
codings, and pointwise combinations. The Thue–Morse sequence realises the
criterion with a kernel of exactly two elements, and its parity form was matched
term-by-term to its multiplicative sign form. The directions below are the
sharpest testable questions these findings raise.

## 1. Exact kernel size equals the minimal automaton's state count

**Conjecture.** For every base `k ≥ 2` and every `k`-automatic sequence, the
number of distinct decimations equals the number of states of the minimal
deterministic automaton that generates it; consequently a sequence with a
kernel of size `m` cannot be generated by any automaton with fewer than `m`
states.

*The key insight is* that decimations are not merely *witnesses* of automaticity
but are in canonical bijection with the reachable states of the syntactic
automaton, so counting decimations is a state-minimisation algorithm in disguise.

*Why now?* The composition law proved this cycle gives decimations the structure
of a monoid action; state minimisation is exactly the orbit-counting problem for
that action, which is now within reach of an elementary argument rather than an
automata-theoretic one.

## 2. Product bases: kernel finiteness is multiplicative

**Conjecture.** A sequence is simultaneously `k`-automatic and `ℓ`-automatic for
multiplicatively independent `k, ℓ` only when it is eventually periodic, and in
that case its `k`-kernel and `ℓ`-kernel have sizes that are both bounded by the
eventual period.

*The key insight is* that the two decimation monoids generate incompatible
scaling symmetries unless the sequence already has a translation symmetry, so
double-automaticity forces periodicity — a finite-kernel avatar of Cobham's
theorem.

*Why now?* With closure under pointwise operations and a clean finiteness
criterion in hand, the difference sequence `n ↦ a(n+1) − a(n)` can be analysed
inside the same framework, turning Cobham's dichotomy into a statement about the
intersection of two finite kernels.

## 3. Closure under Cauchy convolution modulo a prime

**Conjecture.** If `a` and `b` are `p`-automatic with values in `ℤ/p`, then the
running-sum sequence and, more strongly, the mod-`p` Cauchy convolution
`n ↦ Σ_{i≤n} a(i)·b(n−i)` are again `p`-automatic.

*The key insight is* that mod-`p` convolution interacts with base-`p` decimation
through a carry-free "digit convolution" identity, so the convolution's kernel is
a finite image of the product of the two input kernels.

*Why now?* The catalog already isolates the Thue–Morse convolution powers and
their exact parities; combining those explicit parity formulas with the kernel
closure results proved here makes the convolution's finite-kernel bound concrete
and checkable on small cases first.

## 4. A finiteness dichotomy for the value set

**Conjecture.** A sequence has a finite `k`-kernel **iff** both its value set is
finite and each of the finitely many "colour classes" `{n : a(n) = c}` is a
`k`-recognisable set of integers; neither condition alone suffices.

*The key insight is* that the finite-alphabet property proved this cycle is only
*half* of automaticity — the other half is that each preimage is itself described
by an automaton, and the two halves are logically independent.

*Why now?* The evaluation-at-zero map from the kernel to the value set, made
explicit this cycle, is precisely the bridge that lets one separate "few values"
from "structured preimages" and test the two conditions independently.

## 5. Transcendence from two-state kernels

**Conjecture.** Any non-eventually-periodic sequence whose `2`-kernel has exactly
two elements generates, over `ℝ`, a transcendental power series; Thue–Morse is
the extremal representative of this family.

*The key insight is* that a two-element kernel forces a strict self-similar
functional equation of degree two for the generating function, and such an
equation is incompatible with algebraicity over `ℚ(x)` unless the sequence is
periodic.

*Why now?* Having pinned the Thue–Morse kernel to a precise two-element set, the
functional equation `G(x) = G(x²)·(1−x) + …` can be written down exactly, so the
transcendence question becomes an explicit algebraic-independence test rather
than an asymptotic estimate.

# Future Directions — Bruhat order and closure of orbit strata

This cycle established the order-theoretic backbone of the statement *"Bruhat order
preserves closure relations for orbit strata on a product of flag manifolds"*: the
Ehresmann rank criterion is a genuine partial order (its rank matrix determines the
permutation), it is inversion-invariant, it has explicit extremes, and it transports to
a product order via the two-projection map `w ↦ (w, w⁻¹)`. Building on the surviving
results and the failure analysis, we propose the following conjectures.

## 1. The closure order is exactly the componentwise Bruhat order — with matched gradings

**Conjecture.** For the two-projection parametrisation of orbit strata, `O₁ ⊆ closure O₂`
holds if and only if the parametrising pairs satisfy the componentwise Bruhat order, *and*
the codimension of a stratum equals the sum of the two Coxeter lengths of its parameters.

*The key insight is* that the inversion length is a rank function for the Bruhat order, so
the componentwise order on pairs is graded by the *sum* of the two lengths; a closure
relation can only add codimension, which forces the order to be the componentwise one with
additive grading. *Why now?* The transpose identity `rk w⁻¹ i j = rk w j i` proved this
cycle makes the two projections carry perfectly compatible, additively-graded orders, so
the additive-codimension refinement is now within reach rather than conjectural folklore.

## 2. Length monotonicity strengthens to strict length monotonicity on covers

**Conjecture.** If `u < v` in the Bruhat order then `len u < len v`, and every covering
relation `u ⋖ v` increases the length by exactly one.

*The key insight is* that the rank matrix changes by a controlled amount across a single
transposition, so the length gap along a saturated chain telescopes to the number of steps.
*Why now?* We have both the rank criterion and an independent inversion-length statistic
formalised on the same objects (`rk` and `len`), so the two can finally be compared step by
step rather than only at the extreme points (identity and reversal).

## 3. Self-duality of the orbit poset under `w ↦ w₀ w`

**Conjecture.** Multiplication by the reversal permutation `w₀` is an order-reversing
involution of the Bruhat order, and hence the product orbit poset is self-dual: the closure
poset is anti-isomorphic to itself.

*The key insight is* that `w₀` swaps the roles of "smallest positions/values" and "largest
positions/values", turning the maximal rank matrix into the minimal one. *Why now?* With the
identity and reversal already pinned down as the two extremes of the order, the involution
sending one extreme to the other is the natural next structural symmetry to certify.

## 4. Rank-matrix rigidity governs the whole closure lattice

**Conjecture.** Two orbit strata coincide if and only if their rank matrices agree
entrywise, and the closure lattice of strata embeds order-preservingly into the lattice of
entrywise-dominated integer matrices.

*The key insight is* that antisymmetry — "the rank matrix determines the permutation" — is
not just a technical nicety but the reason the closure relation is a *lattice* order rather
than a mere preorder. *Why now?* The determinacy result is now a theorem, so the passage
from "orbits" to "matrices" is a faithful encoding, and the lattice structure can be studied
purely combinatorially.

## 5. Inversion-freeness detects the dense open stratum

**Conjecture.** A stratum is the unique dense (open) orbit of its factor exactly when the
corresponding parameter is inversion-free, and dually the unique closed orbit corresponds to
the reversal parameter.

*The key insight is* that the Bruhat-minimal element is precisely the unique inversion-free
permutation, so "minimal in closure order" and "no inversions" are the same condition. *Why
now?* This cycle proved `bruhat_bot_iff_len_zero`, tying the order-theoretic minimum to the
vanishing of the inversion statistic; extending it from the extreme stratum to a full
open/closed dichotomy is the immediate structural sequel.

# Future Directions — Tightness of the Isolation Lemma under edge offsets

This cycle established, for the singleton hypergraph with an arbitrary integer
edge offset, an exact product–sum formula for the number of isolating weight
assignments, and identified its two extreme regimes: constant offsets reproduce
the Faber–Harris extremal value `n · ∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}`, while widely separated
offsets isolate every assignment and reach the maximum `d^n`. The following
conjectures extend these findings.

## Conjecture 1 — Offset monotonicity of the isolating count

For the singleton hypergraph, the isolating count is minimised exactly at the
constant offsets: every integer offset `f` satisfies
`I(n,d,f) ≥ n · ∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}`, with equality iff `f` is constant.

The key insight is that spreading the offsets apart can only *break* ties in
favour of a unique minimiser, never create them, so the symmetric offset sits at
the bottom of the count and any deviation strictly increases the number of
isolating assignments. Why now? The exact product–sum formula reduces the claim
to a term-by-term comparison of "above threshold" cardinalities against their
symmetric baseline, turning a global extremal statement into a local, checkable
inequality.

## Conjecture 2 — Full offset spectrum

As `f` ranges over all integer offsets, the isolating count `I(n,d,f)` takes
*every* integer value in the interval `[ n · ∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}, d^n ]` and no value
outside it.

The key insight is that the constant and separated offsets realise the two
endpoints, and interpolating one coordinate of the offset at a time changes the
count by controlled increments, sweeping out the whole interval. Why now? Both
endpoints are now pinned down exactly, so the remaining task is a connectivity
argument on the offset lattice rather than a search for the extremes.

## Conjecture 3 — General inclusion-free hypergraphs attain the lower bound

For every inclusion-free hypergraph `H` on `n` vertices there exists an edge
offset `f` for which the number of isolating assignments equals the Faber–Harris
lower bound `n · ∑_{j<d} j^{n-1}` exactly.

The key insight is that a carefully chosen offset can force every edge except a
minimal "spanning skeleton" to be non-competitive, reducing the isolating
structure of an arbitrary Sperner family to that of the singleton hypergraph
already solved here. Why now? The singleton case is the offset-free anchor; with
its exact count in hand, the general statement becomes a question of transporting
that count along an offset that collapses `H` onto its skeleton.

## Conjecture 4 — Real versus integer offsets

The set of isolating-count values achievable with real offsets coincides with
the set achievable with integer offsets; passing to the reals adds no new counts.

The key insight is that the isolating condition depends only on the linear order
of the finitely many edge weights, and any real offset can be perturbed to a
rational — then cleared to an integer — without crossing a tie. Why now? The
integer theory is now exact, so the reduction from real to integer offsets is the
only missing link to the full real-valued Isolation Lemma statement.

## Conjecture 5 — Offset that maximises uniqueness margin

Among all offsets achieving the maximal count `d^n`, the separated offset
`f i = i·d` minimises the total number of distinct edge-weight values used, and
is optimal for the "isolation margin" (the smallest gap between the minimum edge
weight and the runner-up) in a precise `1/`-scaling sense.

The key insight is that geometric separation by exactly the vertex range `d` is
the tightest spacing that still guarantees a global order of edges independent of
the assignment. Why now? The separated construction is already shown to saturate
the count; quantifying *how efficiently* it does so is the natural next question
and connects the counting bound to the quantitative margin that the Isolation
Lemma is usually applied through.
title: This cycle established, for the singleton hypergraph with an arbitrary integer

# Future Directions — The Topology of Argumentation (VI): the existence gap for stable extensions

This cycle (contrarian mode) attacks the **existence gap** left open by the
previous cycle's `Catalog/Novelty/ArgumentationStable.lean`:

> Unlike preferred extensions, **stable extensions need not exist.**

New self-contained file: `Catalog/Novelty/ArgumentationStableGap.lean`
(Lean 4 / Mathlib `v4.28.0`, no `sorry`, axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice`,
`Quot.sound`).

## Bold conjectures, settled

We formulated four bold conjectures on the existence of stable extensions and
settled each — proving two and disproving two.

| # | Conjecture | Verdict | Theorem |
|---|------------|---------|---------|
| C1 | Every finite framework has a stable extension | **DISPROVED** | `no_stable_cycle3` |
| C2 | Every preferred extension is stable | **DISPROVED** | `cycle3_preferred_not_stable` |
| C3 | Every finite symmetric irreflexive framework has a stable extension | **PROVED** | `stable_exists_of_finite_symmetric_irrefl` |
| C4 | Symmetry alone suffices for existence (C3 without irreflexivity) | **DISPROVED** | `no_stable_reflAF` |

### C1 / C2 — the odd cycle refutations

The directed 3-cycle `cycle3 : 0 → 1 → 2 → 0` (`R a b ↔ b = a + 1` on `Fin 3`) is
irreflexive (`cycle3_irreflexive`) and *not* symmetric (`cycle3_not_symmetric`).

* `no_stable_cycle3` — the 3-cycle has **no** stable extension, refuting C1.
* `stable_cycle3_ncard` — quantitatively, `#{stable extensions} = 0` (contrast
  the count `n` for the complete conflict graph in `ArgumentationStable.lean`).
* `cycle3_admissible_empty`, `cycle3_preferred_empty` — the empty set is the
  unique admissible set, hence a preferred extension of the 3-cycle.
* `cycle3_empty_not_stable`, `cycle3_preferred_not_stable` — but `∅` is not
  stable, so `stable ⊊ preferred` is a **strict** inclusion (refuting C2 and
  sharpening `ArgumentationStable.stable_preferred`).

### C3 — existence on the symmetric side

* `exists_maximalConflictFree` — on a finite type a maximal conflict-free set
  (a facet of `K(AF)`) always exists.
* `maximalConflictFree_stable_of_symmetric` — in a symmetric irreflexive
  framework every facet is stable (re-proved self-contained).
* `stable_exists_of_finite_symmetric_irrefl` — hence **every finite symmetric
  irreflexive framework admits a stable extension**, closing the existence gap
  on the symmetric side.

### C4 — irreflexivity is necessary

* `no_stable_of_reflexive` — any nonempty framework in which every argument
  attacks itself has no stable extension (only `∅` is conflict-free, and `∅`
  cannot dominate a nonempty universe).
* `no_stable_reflAF` — the concrete symmetric one-argument self-attack framework
  `reflAF` therefore has no stable extension: symmetry alone does not save C3;
  irreflexivity is genuinely needed.

## Computational evidence

`ComputationalEvidence.md` records the brute-force enumeration over all subsets
of `Fin 3` that motivated these results: the 3-cycle has `1` admissible (the
empty set), `1` preferred, and `0` stable extensions, while the complete graph
`K_3` has `3` stable extensions.

## Open directions

* **Characterize existence in general.** Give a purely combinatorial criterion
  (beyond symmetry) on `(A, R)` guaranteeing a stable extension; e.g. relate it
  to the absence of odd directed cycles among self-defended arguments, or to the
  independence complex of the underlying conflict graph having a full-dimensional
  facet.
* **Counting the gap.** For random or structured frameworks, study
  `#{preferred} − #{stable}` as a numeric invariant of the "abstention" forced
  by odd cycles.
* **Topology of non-existence.** Interpret the vanishing of stable extensions
  (`stable_cycle3_ncard = 0`) homologically: relate it to the reduced homology
  of `K(AF)` for directed (non-symmetric) frameworks, extending the Euler bridge
  of `ArgumentationSymmetric`/`ArgumentationStable` beyond the symmetric case.

# Future Directions: The Algebraic Core of Four-Dimensional Geometry

This cycle isolated two identities — the continuous sum-of-squares identity
`(a+b)² = 4ab + (a−b)²` and the discrete binomial identity
`∑ₖ (−1)ᵏ C(n,k) 2ⁿ⁻ᵏ = 1` — and showed that between them they organize the
complex structure on `ℝ⁴`, the Hopf map, the Clifford torus balance, the cube
Euler characteristic, and the volume/surface relation for the four-ball. The
following conjectures push each strand further.

## 1. Every block-diagonal quarter-turn structure is the canonical fixed-point-free isometry of its odd sphere

The map `J` on `ℝ⁴` squares to `−I`, preserves the norm, and fixes only the
origin. We conjecture that on `ℝ^{2n}` the analogous coordinate-pairing
quarter-turn is, up to orthogonal conjugacy, the *unique* isometry whose square is
central and which acts freely on `S^{2n−1}`, and that every fixed-point-free linear
isometry of an odd sphere is orthogonally conjugate to a block sum of planar
rotations.

The key insight is that fixed-point freeness on the sphere is exactly the absence
of the eigenvalue `1`, and among such maps the ones squaring to a scalar are
forced to be quarter-turns block by block. Why now? The four-dimensional case is
settled here by an explicit `J` with a one-line fixed-point argument, giving a
concrete base case from which the block induction can proceed.

## 2. The balanced torus is the unique area extremum on every radius simplex

On the constraint `∑ rᵢ² = 1` the product controlling the flat-torus area equals
`1 − Σ(rᵢ² − r̄²)`-type deviations, and this cycle proved the two-radius case:
`4 r₁² r₂² = 1 − (r₁² − r₂²)²`, maximal exactly at `r₁² = r₂² = ½`. We conjecture
that on `S^{2m−1}` the symmetric point `rᵢ² = 1/m` is the unique critical point of
the product functional, and the unique embedding invariant under the diagonal
circle action.

The key insight is that the balance condition is algebraically equivalent to the
vanishing of every pairwise squared deviation, which is precisely the
Euler–Lagrange condition for the area under the sphere constraint. Why now? The
exact balance identity is available in closed form, reducing the variational
uniqueness to a symmetric-function optimization.

## 3. The alternating face sum computes the Euler characteristic of every simple polytope boundary

The `n`-cube boundary has Euler characteristic `1 − (−1)ⁿ`, obtained here by
deleting the single top cell from a contractible alternating sum equal to `1`. We
conjecture the same value governs the boundary of *every* simple `n`-polytope,
independent of combinatorial type, through a deformation to the cube's face
lattice.

The key insight is that the alternating face sum is a homotopy invariant of the
boundary sphere `S^{n−1}`, so it cannot depend on the polytope's fine
combinatorics. Why now? The cube case is proved from the binomial theorem alone,
exposing the invariant in its simplest possible form and inviting a
deformation-invariance argument.

## 4. Differentiating the volume law recovers the entire sphere-area hierarchy

This cycle proved `d/dr [(π²/2) r⁴] = 2π² r³`, i.e. the derivative of the
four-ball volume is exactly the three-sphere surface measure. We conjecture the
full coarea tower `d/dr Vol_n(r) = Area_{n−1}(r)` holds dimension by dimension,
with the Gamma-function constants `π^{n/2}/Γ(n/2+1)` linked across dimensions by a
single differentiation, and that the four-dimensional case saturates a sharp
isoperimetric ratio with extremal constant `π²/2`.

The key insight is that the volume constant `π²/2 = π²/2!` is exactly the value
that makes the isoperimetric ratio scale-invariant in dimension four, and
differentiation transports this scaling to the surface constant. Why now? The
exact volume constant and its derivative are established here, so the remaining
step is to match the constants against the surface measure across dimensions.

## 5. The Hopf sphere identity is the shadow of a norm-multiplicativity law

The Hopf image lies on the sphere of radius `|z|² + |w|²` because
`|2z\bar w|² + (|z|² − |w|²)² = (|z|² + |w|²)²`, a direct instance of the core
identity. We conjecture this is the degree-two case of a family of
norm-multiplicative "sum-of-squares" compositions (the Hurwitz–Radon phenomenon),
with the four-dimensional Hopf map corresponding to quaternionic norm
multiplicativity and the eight-dimensional analogue to the octonionic one.

The key insight is that the sphere identity is precisely `‖xȳ‖ = ‖x‖‖y‖` written
in real coordinates, so the Hopf fibration inherits its structure from the
normed division algebras. Why now? The core identity and the sphere-landing
statement are both available in exact form, making the bridge to composition
algebras a direct coordinate computation.
title: This cycle isolated two identities — the continuous sum-of-squares identity

# Future Directions — Fractional-slope reductions of crystalline representations

These conjectures are distilled from the arithmetic/linear-algebra decomposition
established in this cycle: a fractional Frobenius slope is a purely valuation-theoretic
obstruction to reducibility, decoupled from the residual squareness criterion.

## Conjecture 1 — Slope-parity refinement of irreducibility

For odd `p`, even `k ≥ 2`, and `a_p` with `0 < v(a_p) < (k−1)/2` and denominator of
`v(a_p)` coprime to `p`, the semisimplified reduction is irreducible, and its restriction
to inertia is a fundamental character of level equal to the denominator of the slope.

The key insight is that the denominator of the Newton slope, not merely its
non-integrality, controls the tame level of the residual representation, so
irreducibility is refined into a precise inertial type prediction.

Why now? The Newton-slope pair and its non-integrality propagation are now pinned down
exactly, isolating the denominator as the single arithmetic invariant left to interpret
on the Galois side.

## Conjecture 2 — Uniform bound removing the "bad congruence class" hypothesis

For every fractional slope `< p − 2` there is an explicit weight bound `k₀(p, v(a_p))`,
polynomial in `p`, above which irreducibility holds for *all* even `k ≥ k₀` with no
exceptional congruence classes of `k mod p`.

The key insight is that the exceptional classes arise only from the balanced Newton
case `v(a_p) ≈ (k−1)/2`, which the strict sub-balanced bound excludes uniformly once
`k` is large relative to the slope.

Why now? The distinctness of the two slopes was shown to depend solely on the strict
bound `2·v(a_p) < k−1`, suggesting the exceptional classes are an artefact of proximity
to the balanced point rather than a genuine arithmetic obstruction.

## Conjecture 3 — Discriminant non-square density on the residual line

As `k` ranges over even residues mod `2(p−1)` with fixed fractional slope, the residual
Frobenius traces equidistribute, and the proportion yielding an irreducible reduction
tends to `(p−1)/(2p)`, the density of quadratic non-residues in `𝔽_p`.

The key insight is that once the integral (Wach) structure fixes the slope, the residual
representation behaves like a random quadratic over `𝔽_p`, so irreducibility frequency is
governed by non-residue density rather than by the crystalline data.

Why now? The cross-domain bridge proved here — roots exist iff the discriminant is a
square — makes the residual side a clean quadratic-residue question, ready for an
equidistribution statement.

## Conjecture 4 — Cross-slope rigidity

Two crystalline data of the same even weight `k` whose fractional slopes have different
denominators can never have isomorphic semisimplified reductions.

The key insight is that the slope denominator is an isomorphism invariant of the residual
representation (via its inertial level), so distinct denominators force distinct reductions
regardless of the traces `a_p`.

Why now? With the slope pair and its integrality behaviour fully characterised, the
denominator emerges as a candidate complete invariant, inviting a rigidity test.
title: These conjectures are distilled from the arithmetic/linear-algebra decomposition

# Future Directions — Causal Loops in Category Theory

This project studies *"causal loops"* in category theory: structures where composition
(or a tensor product) fails to be associative **on the nose** but is repaired by a
canonical invertible `2`-cell, with coherence holding automatically.

## What is now proved

### Prior cycles
* `CausalLoopsBicategory.lean` — coherence is free in a thin category (`monoidalOfThin`),
  the parenthesization category `PTree α` as a concrete non-strict monoidal category, and
  the Catalan census of bracketings.
* `CausalLoops.lean` — the associator-defect calculus, the pentagon obstruction for
  subtraction, almost-monoids, and loop rotation invariance.

### This cycle — `CausalLoopsStrictification.lean`
The new, deeper result is a genuine **strictification theorem** phrased as an equivalence
of categories:

* **`strictify : PTree α ≌ Discrete (List α)`** — the reassociation groupoid `PTree α` is
  categorically equivalent to the *discrete* category on words. This makes precise the
  slogan "when composition loops back, its skeleton is the free monoid `(List α, ++, [])`":
  all the invertible `2`-cells recording how associativity loops back are collapsed, and
  what remains is exactly the underlying word.

Supporting and surrounding results:

* `PTree.iso_iff` — two bracketings are isomorphic iff they share an underlying word
  (coherence = connectedness);
* `PTree.instIsIso` — `PTree α` is a groupoid;
* `F_full`, `F_faithful`, `F_essSurj`, `F_isEquivalence` — the flattening functor is fully
  faithful and essentially surjective, an independent construction of the equivalence via
  the standard criterion;
* `flatten_tensor`, `ofList_append` — the equivalence carries the (non-strict) tensor
  `node` to concatenation of words, exhibiting the free monoid as the skeleton;
* `Shape.card_bracketings` / `card_bracketings_succ` — the census of loops: the number of
  bracketings of `n + 1` factors is `catalan n`, obeying the Segner convolution recurrence;
* `Shape.iso_of_leaves_eq` — bracketings with equally many factors are isomorphic objects.

## Directions not yet pursued

1. **Monoidal strictification.** Upgrade `strictify` from an equivalence of categories to a
   *monoidal* equivalence, with `Discrete (List α)` given its strict monoidal structure from
   `++`. Thinness should again make all coherence data automatic.
2. **Bicategorical form.** Package `PTree` families over a base as a genuine bicategory and
   prove a `2`-categorical strictification.
3. **Tamari lattice.** Refine the discrete groupoid `PTree α` to the Tamari order by keeping
   only right-rotations, and relate the resulting poset to the associahedron.
4. **Beyond thinness.** Replace the thin hypothesis by a weaker "unique-associator" axiom
   and identify exactly when coherence still holds.

# Future Directions — Delta-Petrie Divisibility and Positivity

The Petrie block `𝔭_k = 1 + x + ⋯ + x^{k-1}` divides `xⁿ − 1` exactly when `k ∣ n`.
This cyclotomic criterion is the arithmetic skeleton of the positivity dichotomy for
the delta-operator family `Δ_{e_j} G(k,n)`. The following conjectures push the
skeleton toward the full multivariate statement.

## Conjecture 1 — Uniform delta-operator dichotomy
For all `k ≥ 2`, `n ≥ 1`, and `1 ≤ j ≤ n`, the symmetric function `Δ_{e_j} G(k,n)`
is Schur positive if and only if `k ∣ n`.
**The key insight is** that the divisibility line does not depend on the elementary
input `e_j`: the same `k ∣ n` threshold that makes `𝔭_k` divide `xⁿ − 1` also controls
the sign pattern of the entire delta family, so `j` is a spectator variable.
**Why now?** The `∇ = Δ_{e_n}` case and its iterates are already settled; isolating the
cyclotomic mechanism shows the argument never used `j = n`, making the uniform version
the natural next target.

## Conjecture 2 — Roots-of-unity certificate for Schur positivity
The failure of Schur positivity of `Δ_{e_j} G(k,n)` when `k ∤ n` is detected by a single
evaluation at a primitive `k`-th root of unity: some Schur coefficient changes sign in
lockstep with `𝔭_k(ζ) = 0`.
**The key insight is** that positivity obstructions are localized at nontrivial `k`-th
roots of unity, so a finite root-of-unity test certifies (non)positivity without
expanding the whole Schur basis.
**Why now?** The proven block-vanishing lemma turns an infinite positivity check into a
finite spectral one, which is exactly the kind of certificate modern symmetric-function
software can verify at scale.

## Conjecture 3 — Cyclotomic factorization of the Petrie function
In the Schur basis, `G(k,n)` factors through the cyclotomic divisors `Φ_d` of `𝔭_k`, and
the `{−1,0,1}` Petrie coefficients are governed by which `Φ_d` survive after applying
`Δ_{e_j}`.
**The key insight is** that the three-valued Petrie coefficients are shadows of the
squarefree cyclotomic factorization `𝔭_k = ∏_{d∣k, d>1} Φ_d`, so coefficient signs are
determined divisor-by-divisor.
**Why now?** With the divisor structure of `𝔭_k` made explicit, the coefficient bound
becomes a statement about products of cyclotomics, a setting with mature tools.

## Conjecture 4 — Iterated `∇^r` sharpening
For the iterate `∇^r G(k,n)`, Schur positivity holds if and only if `k ∣ n`, independent
of `r ≥ 1`.
**The key insight is** that iterating the delta operator preserves the `k ∣ n` threshold
because each application rescales coefficients by factors that vanish precisely at the
same roots of unity.
**Why now?** The single-application uniform result (Conjecture 1) provides the base case;
the roots-of-unity certificate (Conjecture 2) supplies the inductive step.

## Conjecture 5 — Word-count normalization
The principal specialization `P(k,N;1) = k^N` is the unique normalization under which the
`Δ_{e_j}`-images of `G(k,n)` have integer Schur content summing to a `k`-power exactly when
`k ∣ n`.
**The key insight is** that the word-count `k^N` is the "total mass" whose `k`-divisibility
mirrors the Schur-positivity threshold, tying enumeration directly to positivity.
**Why now?** The specialization identity is now proven, so the enumerative side of the
correspondence is on firm ground and ready to be matched against Schur data.
